common_name: Byron Beauty Passionflower (USDA Hybrid Frilled Lavender-Purple Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Byron Beauty is a USDA breeding-program hybrid that flowers earlier in the season than many passionflower hybrids.

directions: Byron Beauty was bred by USDA researchers in the late 1970s from a cross combining native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with several purple-fruited Passiflora edulis selections, and it carries some of the native parent's cold tolerance even though its top growth is only reliably hardy to about 41 degrees Fahrenheit. The large, frilly 4-5 inch flowers pair lavender-blue petals with a densely ruffled purple-and-white corona, opening earlier in the season than many other hybrid passionflowers and continuing heavily through summer. Give it a sturdy trellis or fence in full sun, since it is a vigorous climber reaching 10 feet or more in a single season, and mulch the crown heavily in zone 8b-9 gardens where cold snaps may kill it back to the roots. Like other Passiflora hybrids with maypop parentage, it serves as a larval host for Gulf fritillary butterflies.

common_name: Star of Bristol Passionflower (Lilac-and-White Striped Hardy Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Star of Bristol is a cross of Amethyst and Constance Eliott bred for hardier, alternating lilac-and-white striped flowers.

directions: Star of Bristol was raised by crossing the deep-purple Amethyst hybrid with the hardy white-flowered Constance Eliott selection of blue passionflower, producing thin, alternating lavender-and-white banded petals around a fringed corona that gives the bloom a distinctive striped look. It flowers from summer into fall on a fast-growing, semi-evergreen vine that tolerates part shade better than most passionflower hybrids while still blooming best in full sun. Established roots survive brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit, so in zone 7-8 gardens the vine typically dies back to the ground each winter and resprouts vigorously once the soil warms in spring. Give it a fence, arbor, or trellis with 8-10 feet of lateral room, and expect it to draw pollinators and serve as a Gulf fritillary host plant through its long bloom season.

common_name: Betty Myles Young Passionflower (Vigorous Lilac Hardy Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Betty Myles Young is among the more cold-hardy ornamental Passiflora hybrids, with roots surviving well below freezing.

directions: Bred by British Passiflora specialist Myles Irvine and named for his mother, this hybrid of Passiflora 'Clear Sky' and Passiflora loefgrenii 'Iporanga' produces broad, lightly fragrant, pale-to-deep lilac flowers up to 4.5 inches across, with fine white streaking on the petals contrasting against maroon corona filaments; each bloom stays open for several days rather than the single day typical of many passionflowers. It is unusually cold-hardy for an ornamental hybrid, remaining evergreen through light frost and surviving root-hardy well down into the teens Fahrenheit, so gardeners in zone 7-8 can expect it to die back and resprout reliably rather than being killed outright. The vigorous, tendril-climbing vine needs a sturdy arch, trellis, or fence and produces large, decorative yellow-orange fruit as a bonus alongside its long spring-to-fall bloom season. Like other passionflower hybrids it supports Gulf fritillary butterfly larvae.

common_name: White Wedding Passionflower (Fragrant Pure White Tetraploid Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; White Wedding is a tetraploid hybrid of Constance Eliott bred for larger pure-white flowers on a huskier vine.

directions: German breeder Roland Fischer created White Wedding by crossing the hardy white-flowered Constance Eliott selection of blue passionflower with Passiflora eichleriana, doubling the chromosome count to produce a huskier tetraploid vine with proportionally larger blooms. The fragrant, pure white, 4-inch flowers are ringed by a crown of fine white filaments and appear in flushes from early summer into early fall against lush, lobed, blue-green foliage. It is less cold-hardy than its Constance Eliott parent and can be damaged by hard frost, so in zone 8 gardens it is best sited in a warm, sheltered spot and mulched heavily going into winter, while zone 9-10 gardeners can expect it to stay evergreen most years. Give the rapid-growing vine a fence or pergola with ample room, since it quickly covers structures and, like other Passiflora, serves as a nectar and larval host source for Gulf fritillary butterflies.

common_name: Eynsford Gem Passionflower (Pink-Mauve Victorian Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant near a trellis or obelisk after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil with roots shaded and vines reaching toward sun; Eynsford Gem is a named selection of the classic Victorian-era violacea hybrid group.

directions: Eynsford Gem is one of the named selections within the long-cultivated Passiflora x violacea group of English glasshouse hybrids, distinguished by fragrant, roughly 3-inch flowers in soft pink-mauve tones surrounding a showy crown of white-and-purple banded coronal filaments, greenish-yellow stamens, and three purple stigmas. It is a fast-growing, semi-evergreen climber that flowers in continuous flushes through summer, making it a good choice for a large trellis, obelisk, or container support rather than a fence needing rapid coverage. Like other violacea hybrids it prefers roots kept cool and shaded with the vine itself reaching into part sun to full sun, and it typically dies back to the crown in a hard Gulf Coast winter, resprouting from the roots the following spring in sheltered zone 8b-9 sites. An early spring hard pruning, as with other violacea selections, encourages fuller, more floriferous new growth.

common_name: Guglielmo Betto Passionflower (Cold-Hardy Suckering Pink Hybrid Passion Vine)

planting.note: Plant container vines or rooted suckers after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Guglielmo Betto is an incarnata-parented hybrid that spreads by root suckers and is among the most cold-hardy ornamental Passiflora available.

directions: Named for the Italian author and climbing-plant enthusiast Guglielmo Betto, this hybrid crosses native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with the South American species Passiflora tucumanensis, producing a roughly 2.5-inch flower with soft pink sepals and petals set off by a boldly banded, pinwheel-like corona of pink-and-white filaments. Deeply cut, choppy trilobate leaves give the foliage a distinctive jagged texture compared with the smoother leaves of most passionflower hybrids, and the vine occasionally sets small, good-flavored fruit. Its maypop parentage shows through in an unusually hardy root system that has survived documented winter lows near 0 degrees Fahrenheit and in its habit of sending up abundant new suckering shoots from the roots each spring, even after top growth is killed back by cold. Plant it where the spreading habit can be contained or allowed to naturalize along a sunny fence line, and expect it to support Gulf fritillary butterfly larvae like other Passiflora species.
sources: Passiflora.it — La Collezione Italiana di Maurizio Vecchia
